title: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
summary: How NSA trains sparse attention from scratch with compressed, selected and sliding-window branches and GPU-aligned kernels, and how DeepSeek's DSA picks top-k tokens with a lightning indexer.
outcomes: Explain why post-hoc sparse attention often fails to speed up GQA models or keep quality
Trace NSA's compression, selection and sliding-window branches for one query and count the keys it reads
Compute shared block-importance scores for a GQA group, including the overlap weights of Equation 9
Compute NSA's expected decode speedup from its settings and explain why it is capped near the stride d
Compare DSA's lightning indexer and top-k selection with NSA, and explain why MLA's MQA mode makes it cheap
Write NSA and DSA as masked attention and verify them against dense causal attention
Place NSA among fixed patterns, routing attention, MoBA and InfLLM-v2, and pick a design for a given setting

lessons.title: Why long context needs sparsity, and why bolt-on sparsity disappoints

blocks.md:
Recall from the attention course: a query at position $t$ scores itself against all $t$ earlier keys, takes a softmax, and averages the values. Over a whole sequence of length $L$ that is $O(L^2)$ work. During training and prefill the work is batched into big matrix multiplies, so it is **compute bound**. During decoding, each new token must read the entire KV cache from GPU memory to produce one output, so it is **memory-bandwidth bound**.

The NSA paper (Yuan et al., DeepSeek-AI, Peking University and the University of Washington, 2025) cites theoretical estimates that attention accounts for 70 to 80% of total latency when decoding with a 64k-token context.

The hope is that attention is naturally sparse: for a given query, most of the softmax mass lands on a small set of keys. If we could find those keys cheaply and skip the rest, both compute and memory reads would shrink.

Many methods tried this on top of an already trained, fully dense model: evicting KV entries (H2O, SnapKV), selecting KV blocks per query (Quest, InfLLM), or hashing and clustering keys (MagicPIG, ClusterKV). H2O, short for heavy-hitter oracle, keeps the tokens that have collected the most attention so far plus the most recent ones; Quest and InfLLM keep every entry but load only the blocks that look relevant to the current query; MagicPIG and ClusterKV group similar keys so likely matches can be found without scoring every key. The NSA paper argues these often fail to deliver real speedups, for three reasons.

1. **Phase-restricted sparsity.** Some methods only speed up decoding (H2O) while prefill still pays full cost; others only speed up prefill (MInference, which guesses a sparse attention pattern for each head to process a long prompt faster). One phase stays dense.
2. **Incompatibility with GQA and MQA.** In grouped-query attention, several query heads share one KV cache. If every head picks its own blocks, the GPU must load the *union* of all picks, so memory reads barely drop. Multi-query attention (MQA) is the extreme case: all query heads share a single key and value head.
3. **Not trainable.** Selection is bolted on after pretraining, so the model never learned to work with it. Discrete steps such as k-means clustering (assigning each key to the nearest of a few learned centre vectors) or SimHash block gradients, and token-by-token gathers cannot use FlashAttention-style contiguous tiles.

SimHash hashes a vector by the signs of its dot products with a few random directions, so vectors pointing the same way tend to share a hash; a hash, like a k-means cluster choice, is a discrete jump with no gradient. FlashAttention, the standard fast attention kernel, works through keys and values in contiguous tiles of memory (lesson 4 shows how), so scattered single tokens break it.

blocks.title: Per-head block selection under GQA loads the union

scenes.caption: Four query heads share one KV cache (one GQA group). A Quest-style method lets each head pick its own top 2 of 8 KV blocks. Each head computes on only 2 blocks.
But the KV cache is shared, so the kernel must fetch every block any head wants: the union is 5 of 8 blocks. Compute fell to 2/8 per head, memory traffic only to 5/8.
NSA's fix: all heads in a group agree on one shared selection. Now the group loads exactly 2 blocks, and every loaded block is used by all 4 heads.

blocks.md:
The trainability problem is just as serious. MagicPIG's authors (cited by NSA) found that the top 20% of attention scores cover only about 70% of the total attention mass, so pruning a dense model after the fact throws away real signal. Specialized structures such as retrieval heads are especially fragile. Retrieval heads are the few attention heads that find a fact far back in the context and copy it into the output (Wu et al., 2024), so they depend on a handful of distant keys that a pruner can easily drop.

The conclusion the NSA authors draw: sparsity must be **native**. The model should be trained with the same sparse attention it will use at inference, and the sparse pattern must be shaped around how GPUs actually move memory.

Theoretical FLOP savings are not speedups. A sparse attention method is only fast if the GPU reads fewer bytes in contiguous chunks during every phase (training, prefill, decode), and it only keeps quality if the model is trained with the sparsity.

blocks.question: A model uses GQA with 8 query heads per KV group. A sparse method lets each head choose 4 of 64 KV blocks independently, and the heads mostly disagree. During decoding, roughly what happens to memory traffic per group?
options: It drops to 4/64 of dense, since each head reads 4 blocks
It drops to somewhere up to 32/64 of dense, because the union of the heads' picks must be loaded
It is unchanged, because sparse methods never reduce memory reads
It increases, because sparse methods must read all keys to score them
blocks.explain: Heads in a GQA group share one KV cache, so the kernel loads the union of their selections: up to 8 x 4 = 32 distinct blocks. Compute per head is 4/64, but decoding is memory bound, so the union is what sets latency. This is exactly why NSA forces one shared selection per group.

blocks.question: Why does NSA insist on applying sparsity during pretraining instead of adding it to a finished dense model?
options: Sparse attention cannot run at inference time without training
Dense models have no attention sparsity to exploit
Post-hoc methods use more KV cache memory than NSA
Training with sparsity makes the model's attention patterns adapt to the selection, and it also makes long-context training itself cheaper
blocks.explain: A dense model's attention spreads mass in ways a fixed selector cannot fully capture (top 20% covers about 70% of mass in MagicPIG's measurements). Training natively lets the model learn patterns that fit the selector, and long-context pretraining and fine-tuning also get faster because the forward and backward passes are sparse.

lessons.title: Three branches: compress, select, and slide

blocks.md: NSA keeps the attention formula but changes *what the query attends to*. For each query $q_t$, it builds a small set of remapped keys and values $\tilde K_t, \tilde V_t$ from the full history, and attends only to those. It builds three such sets, one per **branch**, runs ordinary attention on each, and mixes the three outputs with learned gates.

blocks.tex: o_t^{*}=\sum_{c\in\{\text{cmp},\,\text{slc},\,\text{win}\}} g_t^{c}\cdot \operatorname{Attn}\!\left(q_t,\tilde K_t^{c},\tilde V_t^{c}\right),\qquad N_t=\sum_c \operatorname{size}\!\left[\tilde K_t^{c}\right]\ll t
blocks.caption: Equations 5 and 6 of the NSA paper. In words: the output is a gate-weighted sum of three ordinary attention outputs, one per branch. Each gate $g_t^c \in [0,1]$ comes from an MLP with a sigmoid on the input features. Sparsity means the total number of remapped keys $N_t$ is far smaller than $t$.

blocks.md: **Compression (cmp).** Slide a window of length $l$ over the keys with stride $d$, and squeeze each block into one key with a small learnable MLP $\varphi$ that includes an intra-block position encoding. Values are compressed the same way. The query sees about $t/d$ coarse summaries of the whole history. The paper uses $d<l$ (blocks overlap) to avoid cutting information at block edges.

blocks.caption: Equation 7: one compressed key per block of $l$ tokens, blocks spaced $d$ apart. Block $i$ covers tokens $id+1$ to $id+l$ and must end by token $t$, so $i$ runs up to $\lfloor (t-l)/d \rfloor$: about $t/d$ compressed keys.

blocks.md:
**Causality during training.** Training processes every position at once, so the compressed keys of the whole sequence exist side by side. A query at token $t$ may use block $i$ only once the block has ended, $id + l \le t$, which is the upper limit on $i$ in Equation 7. Using a block earlier would let its summary leak tokens from the future.

In the 24-token toy below ($l = d = 4$), the query at token 24 may use all six summaries c0 to c5. A query at token 22 may use only c0 to c4: c5 covers tokens 21 to 24 and has not ended yet. Tokens 21 and 22 still reach that query exactly, through the window branch and the local selection block.

**Selection (slc).** Coarse summaries lose detail, so NSA also picks the $n$ most important blocks of size $l'$ and attends to *every original token* inside them. How the importance is scored is the next lesson. In the paper's configuration $n=16$ includes 1 fixed initial block and 2 fixed local blocks.

**Sliding window (win).** The last $w$ tokens are always attended in full. The authors found local patterns are learned fastest and can dominate training, so giving them a dedicated branch stops them from shortcutting the other two. Each branch even gets its own independent keys and values.

blocks.title: NSA forward pass for one query

scenes.caption: The cached keys and values feed three branches. Each branch builds its own small key/value set for the current query.
The compression branch attends over about t/d compressed keys. This gives a coarse view of the whole history and, as a by-product, a score for every block.
Those scores pick the top-n blocks, whose raw tokens feed the selection branch (dashed edge). No extra scoring network is needed.
The window branch attends to the last w tokens. Three outputs are combined with sigmoid gates computed from the input features.

blocks.title: What one query sees in a 24-token toy (block size 4)

scenes.caption: Toy settings (simplified): $l=l'=d=4$, $n=4$, $w=4$, query at token 24. The real config is $l=32$, $d=16$, $l'=64$, $n=16$, $w=512$.
Compression: tokens are grouped into 6 blocks of 4 and each block becomes one compressed key c0 to c5. The query attends to these 6 summaries.
Selection: block 0 (initial) and block 5 (local) are always kept; the 2 highest-scoring other blocks (here 1 and 2, computed in the next lesson) are added. All 16 of their raw tokens are attended.
Window: the last 4 tokens are attended through their own branch with their own keys and values. Three outputs are computed and mixed by gates.

blocks.prompt: In the toy above, count the keys the query attends to across all three branches. Is that fewer than the 24 keys of full attention?
blocks.reveal:
No. It is 6 compressed + 16 selected + 4 window = **26** keys, more than the 24 of full attention. NSA's cost is roughly $t/d + nl' + w$, and only the first term grows with context length.

With the paper's settings at $t = 65{,}536$: $\lfloor(65536-32)/16\rfloor = 4094$ compressed + $16 \times 64 = 1024$ selected + $512$ window = **5630** keys, about 8.6% of the context. Native sparse attention only pays off at long context.

blocks.md: The gates are independent sigmoids, not a softmax. They do not have to sum to 1, so the model can turn several branches up or down at once. Also note what NSA does *not* do: it keeps the full KV cache (and three branches with independent keys and values), so it cuts the bytes *read* per step, not the bytes *stored*.

blocks.question: A model must copy the token that appeared 3 positions ago. Which NSA branch is designed to make this easy, and why is it a separate branch?
options: Compression, because it summarizes every token
Selection, because top-n scoring always ranks the most recent block first
Sliding window, because local patterns are learned fastest and a dedicated branch keeps them from shortcutting the long-range branches
None; NSA cannot attend to recent tokens exactly
blocks.explain: The window branch attends to the last $w$ tokens in full. The paper isolates it because local patterns adapt quickly and would otherwise dominate the learning signal of the compression and selection branches.

blocks.question: With NSA's settings ($d=16$, $n=16$, $l'=64$, $w=512$), which term of the per-query key count dominates at a 1M-token context?
options: The compressed tokens, about $t/d \approx 65{,}500$
The selected tokens, $nl' = 1024$
The window, $w = 512$
All three are equal
blocks.explain: Selection and window are fixed sizes. Compression grows linearly with $t$ at rate $1/d$, so at long context it dominates: about 65,534 of roughly 67,070 keys at 1,048,576 tokens.

lessons.title: Picking blocks: importance scores come for free

blocks.md: Selection needs a score for every block, and scoring them with a separate network would add cost and need its own training signal. NSA's trick: the compression branch already computed the attention probabilities between $q_t$ and every compressed key. Those probabilities *are* a block-level importance estimate, so they are reused directly.

blocks.caption: Equation 8. When compression and selection blocks coincide, the selection score of block $j$ is simply the compressed attention probability of block $j$.

blocks.md: In the real configuration the blocks do not coincide: compression blocks are $l=32$ tokens with stride $d=16$, and selection blocks are $l'=64$ tokens. The paper's Equation 9 then sums the compressed probabilities of the compression blocks that overlap each selection block (it requires $l \le l'$ and that $d$ divides both $l$ and $l'$). The idea is the same: a selection block is important if the compressed keys covering it got attention.

blocks.caption: Equation 9 as printed. With $l = 32$, $d = 16$ and $l' = 64$ the double sum has 4 x 2 = 8 terms but only 5 distinct compression blocks, so those blocks are weighted 1, 2, 2, 2 and 1.

blocks.md:
Read it by overlap. Cut the sequence into chunks of $d = 16$ tokens. Selection block $j$ (tokens $64j+1$ to $64j+64$) is 4 chunks long; compression block $i$ (tokens $16i+1$ to $16i+32$, Equation 7) is 2 chunks long. Each compression block is counted once for every chunk it shares with the selection block.

For $j = 1$ (tokens 65 to 128) that is compression blocks 3 to 7. Block 3 (tokens 49 to 80) and block 7 (tokens 113 to 144) each share one chunk; blocks 4, 5 and 6 lie fully inside and share two. The paper prints the indices as $4j$ down to $4j-4$, which does not line up with the block numbering of Equations 7 and 12 (that numbering gives $4j-1$ to $4j+3$). A reimplementation should match blocks by position, as lesson 6's code does, and keep the 1, 2, 2, 2, 1 weights.

blocks.title: Which compression blocks feed selection block 1

scenes.caption: Tokens 49 to 144 in 16-token chunks (each cell is one chunk, labeled by its first token). Selection block 1 is the four chunks from token 65 to 128.
Compression block 3 covers tokens 49 to 80: only its second chunk lies inside selection block 1, so it is counted once (weight 1).
Compression block 4 covers tokens 65 to 96, fully inside: weight 2. Blocks 5 (81 to 112) and 6 (97 to 128) are also fully inside and also get weight 2.
Compression block 7 covers tokens 113 to 144: one chunk inside, one in selection block 2. Weight 1 here, and weight 1 again in block 2's score.

blocks.title: One selection score computed by hand

scenes.caption: Illustrative compressed attention probabilities for blocks 3 to 7: 0.04, 0.10, 0.06, 0.03, 0.05.
Multiply by the overlap weights 1, 2, 2, 2, 1: contributions 0.04, 0.20, 0.12, 0.06, 0.05.
Sum: selection block 1 scores 0.47. Scores across blocks add up to about 2, not 1, since each compression block is counted twice in total; only their ranking matters for top-n.

blocks.prompt: Compression block 7 (tokens 113 to 144) gets compressed probability 0.3 and every other block gets 0. What scores do selection blocks 1 (tokens 65 to 128) and 2 (tokens 129 to 192) receive?
blocks.reveal: **0.3 each.** Block 7 shares one 16-token chunk with each selection block, so it is counted once in each: weight 1 in block 1 and weight 1 in block 2. A block lying fully inside one selection block, such as block 5, would instead give 0.6 to that block and nothing to its neighbours.

blocks.md: **GQA sharing.** Heads in a GQA group share one KV cache, so they must agree on one selection (lesson 1). NSA sums the per-head importance vectors over the $H$ heads of the group, then keeps the top-$n$ blocks of the sum:

blocks.caption: Equations 10 and 11. The selected keys are the concatenation of the raw keys of the blocks in $\mathcal I_t$, so the selection branch sees $n l'$ tokens.

blocks.title: Shared block selection for a 2-head GQA group

scenes.caption: Head 1's compressed attention (softmax of illustrative logits 1.0, 0.2, 2.0, 1.6, 0.1, 1.2). On its own it would pick blocks 2 and 3 as its two free choices.
Head 2 (logits 0.8, 1.7, 1.9, 0.0, 0.3, 1.4) prefers blocks 2 and 1. Picked separately, the group would have to load the union: blocks 1, 2 and 3.
Summed over the group: block 2 = 0.678 (from unrounded values), block 1 = 0.322, block 3 = 0.287, block 4 = 0.118. The shared scores rank block 2 then block 1 among the free blocks.
Final selection: blocks 0 (initial, forced) and 5 (local, forced) plus the top 2 of the rest, blocks 2 and 1. Head 1 loses its second choice, block 3, but both heads read the same 4 blocks.

blocks.md: Check the numbers: head 1 gives block 1 only 0.059 and block 3 0.239, while head 2 gives block 1 0.263 and block 3 0.048. Summed, block 1 scores 0.322 and block 3 scores 0.287, so block 1 wins the last slot. The selection is a group compromise, which is exactly what makes the memory reads small.

Top-n selection itself is not differentiable, but NSA does not need it to be. The scores come from the compression branch, which is trained by the ordinary language modeling loss through its own output, and the selected tokens are trained through the selection branch's attention. No auxiliary loss is required.

Two terms first. An **auxiliary loss** is an extra training objective added next to the main one, used to teach one part of a model directly. A **KL loss** uses the Kullback-Leibler divergence, named after Solomon Kullback and Richard Leibler, which measures how far a predicted distribution $q$ is from a target $p$ over the same items: $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\,\|\,q)=\sum_i p_i \log (p_i/q_i)$. Each item adds $p_i$ times the log of how much $q$ under-predicts it, so the divergence is zero only when $q$ equals $p$ and grows when $q$ puts little probability where $p$ puts a lot. It equals the cross-entropy of $q$ against $p$ minus the entropy of $p$, so with a fixed target, minimizing it is the same as minimizing cross-entropy: it pulls $q$ toward $p$.

The paper tested the alternatives on a 3B-parameter model: a learnable selector trained with an auxiliary KL loss against mean-pooled attention scores (the dense attention averaged within each key block), similar in spirit to SeerAttention, which trains a small gate to predict which attention blocks matter, and a parameter-free Quest-style heuristic using the query against the per-block min and max of the keys. Both reached a worse training loss than NSA (Figure 7). The authors also observed that attention in a dense 27B model is blockwise clustered, with neighboring keys getting similar scores, which supports choosing contiguous blocks rather than single tokens.

blocks.question: A teammate proposes letting each of the 16 heads in an NSA GQA group keep its own top-16 blocks, arguing it is more accurate. What is the main cost?
options: The backward pass becomes non-differentiable
Decoding would load the union of up to 256 blocks per group instead of 16, losing most of the memory savings
Compression would no longer work
The window branch would have to grow to compensate
blocks.explain: Heads in a group share KV, so separate selections are loaded as a union. With 16 heads x 16 blocks that can be up to 256 distinct blocks. Summing scores over the group and taking one top-16 keeps reads at 16 blocks while every head uses all of them.

blocks.question: Why does NSA select contiguous blocks of 64 tokens instead of the 1024 individually highest-scoring tokens?
options: Individual tokens cannot be scored
Blocks need less KV cache storage
Token-level selection is not allowed with softmax
Contiguous blocks let neighbouring GPU threads read neighbouring addresses in one wide (coalesced) load and fill Tensor Core tiles, and attention scores tend to be clustered anyway
blocks.explain: GPUs read contiguous memory far faster than scattered indices, and tensor-core matrix multiplies want tiles. The paper also shows attention is blockwise clustered, so blocks lose little. DSA (lesson 5) does select individual tokens, but needs a different kernel design and a separately trained indexer to score them.

lessons.title: Hardware alignment: the kernel and the measured speedups

blocks.md:
FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022) is the standard fast kernel for exact attention. It never writes the full grid of query-key scores out to GPU memory (HBM), which would cost more time than the math. It tiles a *contiguous block of queries* into fast on-chip SRAM (static random-access memory), which the GPU basics course calls shared memory, then streams blocks of keys and values past it. That works because neighboring queries attend to the same keys. With NSA's selection branch, neighboring queries may want *different* KV blocks, so a query tile would trigger scattered, redundant loads.

The compression and window branches are regular, so they reuse FlashAttention-2 kernels (the 2023 second version, which splits the work more evenly across the GPU). For the selection branch, NSA writes its own Triton kernel that groups work differently. Triton is OpenAI's open-source, Python-based language for GPU kernels: you write one program that handles one block of data, and Triton launches a grid of copies of it that the GPU spreads across its streaming multiprocessors.

Streaming keys past the queries needs one trick, the **online softmax**. A softmax needs the largest score (subtracted before exponentiating, to avoid overflow) and the sum of exponentials over all keys, but the kernel sees the keys one block at a time. So for each query it keeps a running maximum $m$, a running sum of $e^{s-m}$ over every score $s$ seen so far, and a running weighted sum of values. When a new block brings a larger maximum $m'$, the old sum and old output are multiplied by $e^{m-m'}$ so everything is on the same scale, then the new block is added. After the last block, dividing the output by the sum gives exactly the softmax-weighted average.

1. **Group-centric loading.** For one query position $t$, load all query heads of the GQA group together. They share the same selected blocks.
2. **Shared KV fetching.** The inner loop walks the selected block indices, loading each contiguous KV block of $B_k$ tokens into SRAM once (with $B_k$ dividing $l'$).
3. **Outer loop on the grid.** Every position has about the same number of selected blocks, so the query loop goes to Triton's grid scheduler and work stays balanced across streaming multiprocessors.

blocks.title: Tracing the selection kernel for the toy query
blocks.code:
# selected-attention forward, one GQA group (simplified)
for t in range(T):            # grid: one program per position
    Q = load(q[t, heads])     # all h heads of the group
    blocks = sel_idx[t]       # shared top-n block ids
    m, l, acc = init_state(h) # online softmax per head
    for b in blocks:          # inner loop
        K = load(k[b])        # contiguous block to SRAM
        V = load(v[b])
        S = Q @ K.T * scale   # [h, B_k] on tensor cores
        m, l, acc = update(m, l, acc, S, V)
    store(o[t, heads], acc / l)

scenes.caption: The grid launches one program per query position. Take the toy query at t = 24 from lessons 2 and 3.
Load both heads' queries together (toy group of h = 2; the paper uses 16 heads per group). They will share every KV load.
Read the shared selection computed in lesson 3: blocks 0, 1, 2 and 5.
First selected block: K and V for tokens 1 to 4 are loaded once as a contiguous tile.
One small matrix multiply scores the block for both heads at once, then the online softmax state is updated, just as in FlashAttention.
After blocks 1, 2 and 5 the loop ends: 4 block loads served 2 heads each. Per-head selection would have loaded blocks 0, 1, 2, 3 and 5.

blocks.md: Why sharing pays, counted. For each of the $B_k$ keys in a block, one head does $d_k$ multiply-adds for the score $q\cdot k$ and $d_v$ multiply-adds to add the probability-weighted value into its output (the PV product, where $P$ holds the softmax probabilities). A multiply-add is 2 floating-point operations, so one head does $2B_k(d_k+d_v)$ FLOPs on the block. The keys and values are stored in bfloat16 (BF16), a 16-bit floating-point format with 2 bytes per number, so loading them costs $2B_k(d_k+d_v)$ bytes. One head gets 1 FLOP per byte loaded; if all $h$ heads of the group reuse the same load, it is $h$ FLOPs per byte. That ratio is the arithmetic intensity from the GPU basics course: higher means each byte fetched from HBM feeds more math.

blocks.caption: Arithmetic intensity of one BF16 KV block load (QK and PV multiply-adds over the bytes of K and V), with the paper's $h=16$ heads per group, $d_k=192$, $d_v=128$ and an assumed $B_k=64$ (it cancels). Loading per head would give 1 FLOP per byte; sharing across the group multiplies it by $h$.

blocks.md:
**Training speed.** On an 8-GPU A100 system, against a Triton FlashAttention-2 kernel, NSA's forward pass was 2.1x faster at 8k tokens rising to 9.0x at 64k, and the backward pass 1.1x rising to 6.0x (Figure 6). Speedups grow with length because dense cost grows quadratically while NSA's grows much more slowly.

**Decoding.** Decoding is memory bound, so speed is roughly proportional to how many tokens of KV are read per step: at most $\lfloor (s-l)/d \rfloor$ compressed tokens, $n l'$ selected tokens, and $w$ window tokens, where $s$ is the cached length.

**The backward pass.** Training also needs gradients. In each branch, the attention backward pass recomputes the probabilities and produces gradients for the queries and for exactly the keys and values that branch read. In the selection branch, only the $n l'$ selected tokens of a query receive key and value gradients from it, and the top-$n$ choice itself receives none: block indices are integers, so the compression branch learns only through its own output (lesson 3).

The hard part is direction. The forward kernel is query-centric: each query position gathers its blocks. Key and value gradients are key-centric: block $b$ must add up contributions from every later query that selected it, and different positions selected different blocks.

So a kernel either scatters partial gradients from many query programs into the same KV block with **atomic adds** (hardware operations that let many threads add into one memory location without losing updates, at the cost of serialized, nondeterministically ordered writes), or it inverts the selection first. The NSA paper does not describe its backward kernel. The open Triton implementation in fla-org/native-sparse-attention takes the second route: it builds a boolean table of which query position selected which block, then runs one program per KV block that walks every later position, checks the table, and accumulates that block's gradients on chip. The walk visits all later positions even when few of them chose the block. That walk shows why a sparse backward pass is harder to make fast than the forward one. The paper's own backward kernel is not public, and the paper gives no breakdown of why its backward speedup trails the forward one.

blocks.title: KV tokens read per decoding step (thousands)

scenes.caption: At 8k context: dense reads 8,192 tokens; NSA reads 510 compressed + 1,024 selected + 512 window = 2,046 (the paper's Table 4 lists 2,048). Expected speedup about 4x. Simplified: time taken as proportional to tokens read.
At 32k: dense 32,768, NSA 2,046 + 1,024 + 512 = 3,582. Expected speedup about 9.1x.
At 64k: dense 65,536, NSA 4,094 + 1,024 + 512 = 5,630 (Table 4: 5,632). Expected speedup about 11.6x, matching the paper's headline decode number.

blocks.title: Expected NSA decode speedup versus context length

scenes.caption: Paper settings ($d=16$, $n=16$, $l'=64$, $w=512$). The points are Table 4. The curve keeps rising with context, but bends toward a ceiling.
Doubling the stride to $d=32$ halves the compressed tokens and raises the ceiling to 32, at the cost of coarser summaries.
Selecting more blocks ($n=32$) lowers the speedup at moderate lengths, but barely matters at 1M tokens, where compressed tokens dominate.

blocks.prompt: With the paper's settings, will NSA's decode speedup keep growing without bound as the context reaches 1M tokens?
blocks.reveal: No. At $s = 1{,}048{,}576$ NSA reads 65,534 compressed + 1,024 + 512 = 67,070 tokens, a speedup of about **15.6x**. Because compressed tokens grow as $s/d$, the speedup can never exceed $d = 16$. At very long contexts the compression branch, not selection, is the cost to attack.

blocks.md: **What it bought in quality.** The paper pretrains a 27B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model (3B active, 30 layers, GQA with 4 groups and 64 heads) with NSA and with full attention. In a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model, each feed-forward layer is split into many expert sub-networks and a small router sends each token to only a few of them, so only 3B of the 27B parameters do work for any one token.

The tests, briefly. The nine general benchmarks cover knowledge, reasoning and coding (for example MMLU, GSM8K and HumanEval). LongBench is a long-context benchmark; the paper reports its single-document and multi-document question answering, synthetic and code tasks. A needle-in-a-haystack test hides one fact (the needle) at some depth in a long filler text and asks the model to retrieve it. AIME 24 is the set of problems from the 2024 American Invitational Mathematics Examination, a hard competition math test, scored as the fraction solved. The distillation step is supervised fine-tuning on 10B tokens of 32k-length math reasoning traces from DeepSeek-R1.

NSA averaged 0.456 versus 0.443 on nine general benchmarks, 0.469 versus 0.437 on LongBench, retrieved perfectly in a 64k needle-in-a-haystack test, and after distillation on reasoning traces scored 0.121 versus 0.046 on AIME 24 with an 8k generation limit. These are one paper's results at one scale; treat them as evidence that native sparsity need not cost quality, not as a guarantee.

blocks.question: Why does NSA's selection kernel loop over GQA groups at each query position, instead of tiling a block of consecutive queries like FlashAttention?
options: Consecutive queries can select different KV blocks, so a query tile would cause scattered, redundant loads, while heads of one group share exactly the same blocks
Triton cannot tile over the query dimension
It reduces the number of compressed tokens
It makes the selection differentiable
blocks.explain: Within a group, every head reads the same selected blocks, so each contiguous block load is reused h times. Consecutive positions have no such guarantee, so tiling them would not share loads.

blocks.question: At 64k context NSA's backward speedup (6.0x) is lower than its forward speedup (9.0x) and its expected decode speedup (11.6x). Which explanation fits the mechanism?
options: NSA disables sparsity in the backward pass
Decoding uses a larger window
Decoding is memory bound, so its speedup tracks the ratio of tokens read, while training passes are compute bound and include the dense-kernel compression and window branches plus extra gradient work
The forward pass skips the compression branch
blocks.explain: Decode latency is set by bytes read, so it follows the 65,536 / 5,630 ratio. The paper does not break down the training gap, but forward and backward are compute bound, include all three branches, and the backward pass adds gradient work for Q, K and V, so the achieved speedup is smaller than the pure read ratio.

lessons.title: DeepSeek Sparse Attention: a lightning indexer picks tokens

blocks.md:
DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) is the sparse attention used in DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp and DeepSeek-V3.2. According to the V3.2 paper, it is the *only* architectural change from DeepSeek-V3.1-Terminus, and it was added by continued training of that dense checkpoint rather than by pretraining from scratch.

DSA keeps NSA's goal and its key systems lesson (all query heads must share one selection) but drops the three-branch design. Instead it uses two parts: a cheap **lightning indexer** that scores every past token, and a **top-k selector** that keeps the $k$ best *individual tokens* for the main attention.

This course stops at V3.2. DeepSeek's 2026 successor, DeepSeek-V4, uses a hybrid of Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) and Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA), and DeepSeek reports that DeepSeek-V4-Pro needs about 10% of V3.2's KV cache at 1M tokens, so unlike NSA and DSA it also shrinks what is stored.

blocks.caption: Equations 1 and 2 of the DeepSeek-V3.2 paper. The query token gives $H^I$ indexer queries and per-head weights; each past token gives one indexer key. ReLU was chosen for throughput.

blocks.md: In words: each indexer head $j$ takes the dot product of its query with token $s$'s indexer key, ReLU clips negative values to zero, and the clipped values are added up with the weights $w$. The main attention then runs from the query token's hidden state $h_t$ over only the cached entries $c_s$ of the $k$ tokens with the highest index scores.

blocks.title: A toy lightning indexer: 2 heads, 6 past tokens, k = 2

scenes.caption: Head 1 (query 1.0, 0.5, -0.5) dotted with six 3-dim indexer keys, then ReLU. Negative matches become exactly 0, so they cannot help a token.
Head 2 (query -0.5, 1.0, 0.5) likes different tokens: 3, 5 and 6. A dense softmax head would mix everything; here each head just votes.
Weighted sum with per-token head weights 0.7 and 0.3 (they come from the query token too). Index scores: 0.175, 0.91, 0.36, 0.49, 0.715, 0.135.
Top-k with k = 2 keeps tokens 2 and 5. Only their key-value entries go into the main attention. In DeepSeek-V3.2, k = 2048 out of up to 128K tokens.

blocks.md: In the released configuration the indexer has 64 heads of dimension 128, runs in FP8 (an 8-bit floating-point format, 1 byte per number, half the size of BF16), and keeps an extra 128-dimension FP8 key per token per layer; top-k is 2048. The main attention is Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA), introduced in DeepSeek-V2. Instead of caching a separate key and value for every head, MLA caches one compressed latent vector $c_s$ per token (512 numbers) plus a 64-number key $k^R_s$ that carries position through RoPE (rotary position embedding, from the attention course), 576 numbers in all. Learned up-projections rebuild each head's content key and value from the latent: for head $i$, $W^{UK}_i c_s$ (128 numbers) and $W^{UV}_i c_s$ (128 numbers). Rebuilding them for every cached token and all 128 heads would be expensive. Regrouping the matrix products avoids it:

blocks.tex: q_{t,i}^{\top}\big(W^{UK}_i c_s\big)=\big(W^{UK\top}_i q_{t,i}\big)^{\top} c_s,\qquad o_{t,i}=W^{UV}_i\Big(\sum_s a_{t,s,i}\,c_s\Big)
blocks.caption: Weight absorption. Map head i's 128-wide content query into the 512-wide latent space once, score it directly against each cached latent (the 64-wide RoPE parts are dotted as they are and added), mix the latents with the attention weights a, then apply the value up-projection once.

blocks.md:
This is the **MQA mode** of MLA (recall from lesson 1: in multi-query attention every query head shares one key and value head). After absorption, all 128 heads score against the same 576-wide rows $[c_s; k^R_s]$ and mix the same 512-wide $c_s$, so one cached row serves every head. DeepSeek's reference code decodes this way, applying $W^{UV}$ after the mixing step. The V3.2 paper builds DSA on this mode for NSA's reason: each key-value entry must be shared across many queries.

It is also what makes token-level top-k affordable. Picking 2048 scattered tokens means gathering 2048 rows of 576 numbers once per query token, not once per head. DeepSeek's FlashMLA library ships token-level sparse kernels that take the list of selected token indices and read those rows directly. For a step-by-step derivation, see the Multi-head latent attention course (not a prerequisite of this one): absorption is its lesson 3 and the decoupled RoPE part its lesson 4.

blocks.title: DSA inside one DeepSeek-V3.2 attention layer

nodes.label:
Indexer key cache
128-d FP8 per token

Index scores
I(t, s) for all s

scenes.caption: Each new token writes two things: its MLA latent KV entry and a small FP8 indexer key. Nothing is evicted; the full history stays cached.
The indexer scores the current query against every cached indexer key. This is still O(L) per query, but with few, small, FP8 heads.
Top-k picks 2048 token positions and gathers only their latent entries. The expensive 128-head attention runs on those 2048 entries, so its cost per query stops growing with L.

blocks.md: **Training the indexer.** Top-k is not differentiable, so DSA gives the indexer its own loss. In a **dense warm-up** (1000 steps of 16 sequences of 128K tokens, about 2.1B tokens, learning rate $10^{-3}$) the main model is frozen and still attends densely. For each query, the main attention probabilities are summed over heads and L1-normalized (divided by their total so they sum to 1) into a target $p_{t,:}$, and the indexer learns to match it.

blocks.caption: Equation 3. In words: for each query, the KL divergence (lesson 3) from the target $p_{t,:}$ to the softmax of the index scores, summed over queries. In the later sparse stage the same KL loss is computed only over the selected set $S_t$.

blocks.md:
Then a **sparse training** stage turns on top-2048 selection and trains everything for 15,000 steps of 480 sequences of 128K tokens (about 943.7B tokens, learning rate $7.3\times10^{-6}$). The indexer's input is detached from the computational graph, meaning gradients stop there: the indexer learns only from its KL loss, and the main model only from the language modeling loss.

Two things follow. The KL loss cannot reshape the main model's hidden states just to make them easier to index, so the indexer has to follow the model and not the other way round. And the language modeling loss never needs a gradient through top-k, which has none. Post-training uses the same sparse attention.

blocks.title: Attention multiply-adds per query: dense MLA vs DSA

scenes.caption: Simplified count from the released config: 139,264 multiply-accumulates (MACs) per attended key for the main attention, 128 heads x (576 score + 512 value), versus 8,192 for the indexer (64 x 128). Ignores FP8 speed and all non-attention layers.

At L = 128K: dense is about 18,254M MACs, DSA about 1,359M, roughly 13.4x less. Below about 2K tokens DSA is no cheaper. For short prefills DeepSeek instead runs a masked MHA mode that simulates DSA, which it reports is more efficient there.
Raising k to 8192 shifts the crossover right and shrinks the long-context gain. The indexer term (x times 8,192) is the floor that no choice of k removes.

blocks.md: Neither NSA nor DSA shrinks the KV cache. NSA adds compressed and per-branch keys; DSA adds an indexer key per token. Both cut the bytes *read and computed* per query. Also, DSA's indexer is still $O(L^2)$ over a sequence, just with a much smaller constant.

**NSA versus DSA in one view.**

- **Granularity:** NSA selects blocks of 64 tokens; DSA selects individual tokens.
- **Scoring:** NSA reuses the compression branch's attention; DSA trains a separate FP8 indexer with a KL loss.
- **Coverage:** NSA adds compressed and window branches for global and local context; DSA relies on top-k alone.
- **Adoption path:** NSA was pretrained from scratch; DSA was retrofitted to a dense checkpoint by continued training.

RoPE (rotary position embedding) encodes position by rotating pairs of query and key dimensions by angles that grow with position. Implementations differ in which dimensions form a pair (neighbours, called interleaved, or the first half with the second half), and the two layouts are not interchangeable. A real-world reminder that details matter: on 2025-11-17 DeepSeek noted that earlier inference demo code applied RoPE in the indexer with the wrong (interleaved) layout, which could degrade outputs.

blocks.question: During DSA's dense warm-up, what is the indexer trained to predict?
options: The next token, using the language modeling loss
Which tokens NSA's compression branch would select
The main attention distribution for each query, summed over heads and L1-normalized, via a KL loss
A binary label for whether each token is in the top 2048
blocks.explain: The target $p_{t,:}$ is the dense main attention summed over heads and normalized. The indexer's softmax is pulled toward it with KL divergence while the main model is frozen, so the indexer learns which tokens the model actually attends to before sparsity is switched on.

blocks.question: Serving cost per token for a DSA model is measured at positions 1K, 32K and 128K. What pattern does the mechanism predict for the attention part?
options: Constant at all positions, since top-k is fixed
Close to dense at 1K, then growing much more slowly than dense, because only the cheap indexer term scales with position
Lower than dense at 1K and identical at 128K
Growing faster than dense because of the indexer
blocks.explain: Below $k$ tokens DSA attends to everything and adds indexer work, so it is no cheaper. Beyond that, the main attention is capped at 2048 entries and only the indexer (about 17x fewer MACs per key in this count) keeps growing with position.

blocks.question: You want sparse attention for a model that will serve 1M-token contexts. Which statement is the best reading of the two designs?
options: NSA's decode speedup grows without limit, so it is strictly better
DSA needs no extra memory per token
Both remove the need to store the full KV cache
Both have a linearly growing per-query term (NSA's compressed tokens, DSA's indexer), so at extreme lengths the cheap scoring path becomes the bottleneck to optimize
blocks.explain: NSA reads about $s/d$ compressed tokens per step, capping its speedup near $d$. DSA's indexer scores all $L$ cached tokens. In both, the scoring or summarizing path scales with context, and both keep the full KV cache.

lessons.title: Write NSA and DSA as masked attention and test them against dense

blocks.md:
The surest test of understanding a mechanism is to write it in the plainest possible form and check it against something you trust. Here the plain form is **masked attention**: every branch is ordinary softmax attention over all keys, plus a boolean mask that says which keys each query may see. A mask is slow, because every score is still computed, but it is exact, so a fast kernel can later be checked against it.

The trusted answer is dense causal attention. If NSA selects every block and only the selection branch is switched on, its output must equal dense attention exactly. Tiny example: with 2 blocks and $n = 2$, the selection mask is all past tokens, which is the causal mask itself.

The setup is one GQA group: $H = 4$ query heads sharing one key and value head of width 16, over $T = 512$ tokens, with the paper's block shapes $l = 32$, $d = 16$, $l' = 64$ and a window $w = 64$. Weights are random and untrained; the point is the bookkeeping, not quality. One simplification: the compression and selection branches share the raw keys and values `k`, `v` here, as the open fla-org kernels do, while the paper gives each of the three branches its own; only the window gets separate `kw`, `vw`.

Part 1 builds the compression branch. `unfold` cuts the keys into 31 overlapping blocks of 32 with stride 16. `Phi` adds a learned position vector to each slot, flattens the block and maps it to one key (the reading from lesson 2). `cmp_mask` lets a query see a block only once the block's last token is in its past.

blocks.code:
import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F
torch.manual_seed(0)
T, H, dk = 512, 4, 16            # one GQA group: 4 query heads, 1 KV head
l, d, lp, w = 32, 16, 64, 64     # cmp block l, stride d, slc block l', window w
q = torch.randn(H, T, dk)
k, v = torch.randn(T, dk), torch.randn(T, dk)     # cmp and slc
kw, vw = torch.randn(T, dk), torch.randn(T, dk)   # window: own K, V
t_ = torch.arange(T)[:, None]                     # query positions (column)
causal = torch.arange(T)[None, :] <= t_

def attend(q, k, v, mask):       # mask [T, N]: True = query may see key
    s = (q @ k.T / dk ** 0.5).masked_fill(~mask, float("-inf"))
    p = s.softmax(-1).nan_to_num()   # a row seeing nothing gives 0
    return p @ v, p

class Phi(nn.Module):            # l keys + intra-block positions -> 1 key
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.pos = nn.Parameter(0.02 * torch.randn(l, dk))
        self.mlp = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(l * dk, 2 * dk), nn.GELU(),
                                 nn.Linear(2 * dk, dk))
    def forward(self, x):
        blocks = x.unfold(0, l, d).transpose(1, 2)    # [nb, l, dk]
        return self.mlp((blocks + self.pos).flatten(1))   # [nb, dk]

with torch.no_grad():
    kc, vc = Phi()(k), Phi()(v)  # separate MLPs for keys and values
nb = kc.shape[0]
ends = torch.arange(nb) * d + l - 1               # last token per block
cmp_mask = ends[None, :] <= t_                    # only complete blocks
print("blocks:", nb, "| visible to tokens 24, 48, 512:",
      [cmp_mask[t - 1].sum().item() for t in (24, 48, 512)])

blocks.md: Part 2 is selection. `W` is Equation 9 written by position: entry $(i, j)$ counts the 16-token chunks that compression block $i$ shares with selection block $j$. `select` turns compressed probabilities into block scores, sums them over the group's heads (Equation 10), pins the initial block and the two local blocks to the top, removes future blocks, and keeps the top $n$: one choice for the whole group. The block mask is then expanded to tokens and intersected with the causal mask, because the block holding the query is only partly in the past.

blocks.code:
ns = T // lp                                      # 8 selection blocks
i, j = torch.arange(nb)[:, None], torch.arange(ns)[None, :]
ov = (torch.minimum(i * d + l, (j + 1) * lp)
      - torch.maximum(i * d, j * lp)).clamp(min=0)
W = ov / d       # Eq. 9: d-token chunks cmp block i shares with slc block j
print("slc block 1 <- cmp blocks", W[:, 1].nonzero().flatten().tolist(),
      "weights", W[:, 1][W[:, 1] > 0].int().tolist())

def select(p_cmp, n):            # p_cmp [H, T, nb] -> token mask [T, T]
    score = (p_cmp @ W).sum(0)                    # Eqs. 9-10: [T, ns]
    cur = t_ // lp
    forced = (j == 0) | (j == cur) | (j == cur - 1)   # initial + 2 local
    score = score.masked_fill(forced, float("inf"))
    score = score.masked_fill(j * lp > t_, float("-inf"))  # future blocks
    top = score.topk(min(n, ns), dim=-1).indices  # one choice per group
    blk = torch.zeros(T, ns, dtype=torch.bool).scatter_(1, top, True)
    blk &= j * lp <= t_                           # drop padded future picks
    return blk.repeat_interleave(lp, dim=1) & causal   # raw tokens, causal

blocks.md: Part 3 adds the window branch with its own keys and values, sigmoid gates (one linear layer on the query stands in for the paper's gate MLP on the input features), and the tests. With $n = 8$ every block is selected, so with the gates fixed to (0, 1, 0) the output must equal dense causal attention. With $n = 4$ later queries skip blocks, so the output must differ. Last, it counts the keys token 512 reads and compares them with lesson 2's formula.

blocks.code:
win_mask = causal & (torch.arange(T)[None, :] > t_ - w)
Wg = torch.randn(dk, 3)          # stand-in gate MLP: one linear layer

def nsa(n, gates=None):
    o_c, p = attend(q, kc, vc, cmp_mask)
    o_s, _ = attend(q, k, v, select(p, n))
    o_w, _ = attend(q, kw, vw, win_mask)
    g = torch.sigmoid(q @ Wg) if gates is None else torch.tensor(gates).expand(H, T, 3)
    return g[..., :1] * o_c + g[..., 1:2] * o_s + g[..., 2:] * o_w

dense, _ = attend(q, k, v, causal)
for n in (8, 4):
    err = (nsa(n, [0.0, 1.0, 0.0]) - dense).abs().max().item()
    print(f"only selection on, n={n}: max |diff| vs dense = {err:.2e}")
print("full NSA output shape:", tuple(nsa(3).shape))

_, p_cmp = attend(q, kc, vc, cmp_mask)
keys = cmp_mask.sum(1) + select(p_cmp, 4).sum(1) + win_mask.sum(1)
print("keys read by token 512 with n=4:", keys[-1].item(),
      "| formula (t-l)//d + 1 + n*l' + w =", (512 - l) // d + 1 + 4 * lp + w)

blocks.md: Part 4 is a DSA-style variant on the same data: four ReLU indexer heads of width 8 with per-query head weights (Equation 1 of the V3.2 paper), a causal top-$k$, and one token selection shared by all four query heads, as MQA mode requires. With $k = T$ it must match dense; with $k = 64$ each query reads at most 64 keys. Part 5 checks lesson 4's backward claim: the gradient of token 512's selection-branch output reaches only the keys it selected.

blocks.code:
HI, dI = 4, 8                    # indexer heads and their width
qI, kI = torch.randn(HI, T, dI), torch.randn(T, dI)
wI = torch.rand(T, HI)           # per-query head weights
I = torch.einsum("tj,jts->ts", wI, F.relu(torch.einsum("jtd,sd->jts", qI, kI)))

def dsa(topk):                   # one token selection shared by all H heads
    sc = I.masked_fill(~causal, float("-inf"))
    top = sc.topk(topk, dim=-1).indices
    m = torch.zeros(T, T, dtype=torch.bool).scatter_(1, top, True) & causal
    return attend(q, k, v, m)[0], m

out, _ = dsa(T)
print(f"DSA with k = T: max |diff| vs dense = {(out - dense).abs().max().item():.2e}")
out, m = dsa(64)
print("DSA with k = 64: token 512 reads", m[-1].sum().item(), "keys; token 40 reads",
      m[39].sum().item(), "| max |diff| vs dense =", round((out - dense).abs().max().item(), 3))

k.requires_grad_(True)           # backward of the selection branch, token 512
o, _ = attend(q[:, -1:], k, v, select(p_cmp, 4)[-1:])
o.sum().backward()
print("keys with nonzero gradient:", (k.grad.abs().sum(1) > 0).sum().item(), "of", T)

blocks.md:
Real output of parts 1 to 5 (CPU, torch 2.15):

```
blocks: 31 | visible to tokens 24, 48, 512: [0, 2, 31]
slc block 1 <- cmp blocks [3, 4, 5, 6, 7] weights [1, 2, 2, 2, 1]
only selection on, n=8: max |diff| vs dense = 0.00e+00
only selection on, n=4: max |diff| vs dense = 5.87e-01
full NSA output shape: (4, 512, 16)
keys read by token 512 with n=4: 351 | formula (t-l)//d + 1 + n*l' + w = 351
DSA with k = T: max |diff| vs dense = 0.00e+00
DSA with k = 64: token 512 reads 64 keys; token 40 reads 40 | max |diff| vs dense = 1.44
keys with nonzero gradient: 256 of 512
```

What each line proves:

- Token 24 sees no compressed block (the first ends at token 32), token 48 sees two, token 512 all 31. Early tokens rely on the window and selection branches.
- Selection block 1 is fed by compression blocks 3 to 7 with weights 1, 2, 2, 2, 1, the hand calculation from lesson 3.
- Selecting everything reproduces dense attention bit for bit; dropping blocks does not.
- Token 512 reads 351 keys against 512 for dense attention. The count uses Equation 7's range, $\lfloor (t-l)/d \rfloor + 1$ blocks; the paper's decode section, and the 64K counts in lessons 2 and 4, use $\lfloor (s-l)/d \rfloor$, one fewer (4,094 rather than 4,095 at 64K), a difference too small to matter.
- The untrained DSA indexer picks tokens unrelated to the attention, hence the large difference at $k = 64$; the dense warm-up of lesson 5 exists to fix that.
- 256 keys get gradient: the 4 selected blocks of 64.

blocks.title: Selection with n = 4 from the run above (8 blocks of 64)

scenes.caption: Five query positions and the eight selection blocks of 64 tokens. Masked cells are future blocks the query may not select.
Forced blocks (value 2): block 0 for every query, plus the block holding the query and the one before it. That uses 3 of the n = 4 slots.
The fourth slot goes to the highest group-summed score among the rest (highlighted). Token 256 has only 4 past blocks, so it sees everything; token 512 skips 4 of 8 blocks.

blocks.md: Lesson 1 quoted MagicPIG's measurement that in dense models the top 20% of attention scores cover only about 70% of the mass. You can measure this on any open model. Qwen2.5-0.5B is small enough for a laptop and uses GQA: 14 query heads and 2 key-value heads, so 7 heads per group. The script reads a text file named on the command line (`python mass.py intro.txt`; it needs at least 2,048 tokens, here the NSA paper's own introduction), feeds its first 2,048 tokens, hooks every layer's attention probabilities, and for query tokens 1,025 to 2,048 reports the softmax mass kept by the top 64 and top 512 single tokens, the top 20% of tokens, and 8 blocks of 64 tokens (512 tokens in all) picked per head or once per GQA group. These picks use the true probabilities, so they are upper bounds that no real selector can beat.

blocks.code:
import torch, sys
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM
name = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B"       # GQA: 14 query heads, 2 KV heads
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(name, attn_implementation="eager",
                                             dtype=torch.float32)
ids = tok(open(sys.argv[1]).read(), return_tensors="pt").input_ids[:, :2048]
assert ids.shape[1] == 2048
B, Q0, G, stats = 64, 1024, 7, []

def hook(mod, args, out):        # out[1]: probs [1, 14, T, T]
    p = out[1][0, :, Q0:]        # tokens 1025..2048 as queries
    srt = p.sort(-1, descending=True).values.cumsum(-1)
    n20 = (0.2 * torch.arange(Q0 + 1, 2049)).long() - 1
    blk = p.unflatten(-1, (-1, B)).sum(-1)  # mass per block
    grp = blk.unflatten(0, (2, G)).sum(1, keepdim=True)
    pick = grp.topk(8, -1).indices.expand(-1, G, -1, -1).flatten(0, 1)
    stats.append([srt[..., 63].mean(), srt[..., 511].mean(),
                  srt.gather(-1, n20.expand(14, -1)[..., None]).mean(),
                  blk.topk(8, -1).values.sum(-1).mean(),  # per head
                  blk.gather(-1, pick).sum(-1).mean()])  # per group
    return out[0], None          # drop probs

for layer in model.model.layers:
    layer.self_attn.register_forward_hook(hook)
with torch.no_grad():
    model(ids)
labels = ["top 64 tokens", "top 512 tokens", "top 20% tokens",
          "8 blocks, per head", "8 blocks, per group"]
for lab, col in zip(labels, torch.tensor(stats).T):
    print(f"{lab:19s} mean {col.mean():.3f}   worst layer {col.min():.3f}")

blocks.md:
Real output (Apple M5 Pro CPU, torch 2.15, transformers 5.24, about 30 seconds):

```
top 64 tokens       mean 0.846   worst layer 0.561
top 512 tokens      mean 0.981   worst layer 0.955
top 20% tokens      mean 0.956   worst layer 0.885
8 blocks, per head  mean 0.896   worst layer 0.648
8 blocks, per group mean 0.879   worst layer 0.611
```

Read it carefully. The top 512 single tokens keep 98.1% of the mass, while 8 blocks holding the same number of tokens keep 89.6%: contiguity cost about 8.5 points in this dense model. Making the 7 heads of a group agree on one pick cost another 1.7 points. The worst layer loses far more (61.1% kept with shared blocks), so averages hide fragile layers. The top 20% kept 95.6% here, well above MagicPIG's roughly 70%: such numbers depend on the model, the layer and the text.

All of this is a dense model scored after the fact. NSA's argument is that a model trained with block selection learns to put its attention where the selector can find it, so these gaps are what post-hoc methods pay, not what a native model pays.

Write the masked reference first. Setting the sparsity knob to select everything must reproduce dense attention exactly, and any fast kernel can then be compared with the reference on random inputs, including its gradients.

This lesson shows no speedup at all: masked attention computes every score, and it ran on a CPU. Speed comes only from kernels that skip unselected blocks, such as the paper's Triton kernel from lesson 4. No GPU timing is shown here; for measured numbers use the paper's A100 results in lesson 4.

blocks.question: Your NSA reimplementation, with n large enough to select every block and gates fixed to (0, 1, 0), differs from dense causal attention, and the error appears inside every selection block except at its last token. What is the most likely bug?
options: The selected block mask was not intersected with the causal mask, so queries see later tokens of their own block
The compression stride d is wrong
The gates should be a softmax, not sigmoids
The window w is too small
blocks.explain: The block holding the query is only partly in the past. Without the token-level causal mask, each query attends to later tokens of its own block; only the block's last token has no later tokens inside it. Compression stride and window do not affect the selection branch output, and the gates are fixed in this test.

blocks.question: Why does `cmp_mask` compare the query position with the last token of each compression block, not the first?
options: Because the last token always has the largest key
To make the compressed keys differentiable
It is arbitrary; either choice gives a valid causal model
Because a summary mixes all l tokens of its block, so using it before the block ends would leak future tokens into the past
blocks.explain: The MLP reads the whole block, so its output depends on every token in it. A query that saw the summary before the block ended would get information from tokens after itself, which breaks causal training and cannot be reproduced at decode time.

lessons.title: Where NSA sits: fixed patterns, routing, MoBA and InfLLM-v2

blocks.md: Every sparse attention method answers one question: for this query, which keys? Picture a query at token 1,000 of a long document. A fixed rule might say: the previous 64 tokens plus every 32nd token before that. A content rule might say: the tokens whose keys look like this query. NSA is a content rule with fixed safety nets attached. Seeing the earlier answers shows which of its choices are essential and which are one option among several.

**Fixed patterns (2019 to 2020).** The Sparse Transformer (Child et al., OpenAI, 2019) factorized attention: one head attends to the previous $l$ positions, another to every $l$-th position, with the stride $l$ close to $\sqrt{n}$, so cost drops to $O(n\sqrt{n})$ and any token is reached in two steps. On text the authors found the strided pattern routed information poorly and used a fixed pattern instead, where a few summary positions at the end of each block are visible to all later positions.

Longformer (Beltagy et al., 2020) combined a sliding window, optionally dilated (skipping positions to widen its reach), with task-chosen global tokens that attend to everything and are attended by everything, for cost linear in length. BigBird (Zaheer et al., 2020) used a window, a few global tokens and $r$ random keys per query, and proved this keeps full attention's theoretical power: it is a universal approximator of sequence functions and Turing complete.

blocks.title: Who may attend to whom: four sparse patterns on 12 tokens

scenes.caption: Sliding window of 3: each query (row) sees itself and the two keys before it. 33 of 78 causal pairs. Cheap and contiguous, but blind beyond the window.
Sparse Transformer, strided (stride 3): the window plus every 3rd earlier token, 51 pairs. Any token is reached in two hops. Simplified: the paper splits the two parts across heads.
Window plus a global token (token 1) plus one random key per row, in the spirit of BigBird: 50 pairs. Simplified: BigBird and Longformer were mainly bidirectional encoders; shown causal here.
Content-based blocks of 3, NSA or MoBA style: block 1, the query's own block, and one block chosen by score (rows 7 to 12). The pattern now depends on the content, not on position alone.

blocks.md:
What fixed patterns get right: they are regular, so kernels read contiguous memory, and they work in every phase. What they miss is content. A fact far back that is not on the pattern can only be reached by hopping through several layers. NSA keeps two of their ideas as safety nets, the sliding window and the always-selected initial block (which plays a role like a global token), and puts content-based choice on top.

**Content-based routing (2020).** Reformer (Kitaev et al.) hashes queries and keys with locality-sensitive hashing (a hash that sends nearby vectors to the same bucket with high probability), sorts tokens by bucket and attends within chunks, for $O(L \log L)$. The Routing Transformer (Roy et al.) groups queries and keys around learned cluster centers (online k-means) and lets each query attend to keys in its cluster, alongside local attention, for $O(n^{1.5}d)$. Both choose by content, but the bucket or cluster choice is discrete, so the loss cannot train it directly, and keys in one bucket sit scattered in memory. These are the two problems lesson 1 listed.

**MoBA (Moonshot AI, 2025)** treats blocks of keys like experts in a Mixture-of-Experts layer. Each query scores every past block by its dot product with the block's mean-pooled key, keeps the top $k$ blocks, and always includes its own current block under a causal mask; future blocks are excluded. The gate has no parameters, so a layer can switch between full attention and MoBA during training, and the authors keep some layers full (the last three of 32 in their 1M-context Llama-8B model, which used blocks of 4096 and top-12). They report up to 6.5x faster prefill at 1M tokens and deployment for Kimi's long-context requests. The paper describes the gate per head; it does not ask the heads of a GQA group to agree.

**InfLLM-v2 (in MiniCPM4, 2025)** scores blocks with parameter-free mean pooling too, but over overlapping kernels of 32 tokens with stride 16 (NSA's compression shape) and takes each block's score as the maximum over the kernels that touch it. Heads in a GQA group average their scores and share one top-$k$, and the initial block and local window are always kept.

InfLLM-v2's selling point is switching. When the input is shorter than $k$ blocks it is exactly dense attention, and because it adds no parameters a model can be pretrained densely on short text and then trained sparse on long text. Its authors criticize NSA's three branches for adding parameters, slowing short inputs and tripling key-value storage in pretraining; the follow-up InfLLM-V2 paper reports 4x faster attention than dense with 98.1% of the performance on long-context understanding and 99.7% on chain-of-thought reasoning.

**Side by side.**

- **Granularity:** NSA, MoBA and InfLLM-v2 pick blocks; DSA picks single tokens.
- **Block scoring:** NSA reuses its trained compression branch; MoBA and InfLLM-v2 use mean-pooled keys (no parameters); DSA trains a separate indexer.
- **Heads share a selection:** NSA, InfLLM-v2 and DSA yes; MoBA as described, no.
- **Training path:** NSA from scratch; DSA retrofitted with a warm-up; MoBA and InfLLM-v2 switch from dense.
- **Kernel:** all need a gather-style sparse kernel; DSA's must gather single tokens.

nodes.label:
DSA indexer warm-up,
or MoBA / InfLLM-v2

scenes.caption: The first question is what you start from, because it decides whether the selector can be trained with the model.
From scratch, NSA-style native training lets the model and its block selection co-adapt, at the price of extra branches and parameters.
From a dense checkpoint, add a cheap selector and keep training: DSA warms up a separate indexer with a KL loss; MoBA and InfLLM-v2 score blocks with mean-pooled keys and add no parameters.
With no training budget, a training-free selector like Quest speeds up decoding only, and the model never adapts to it.
Whatever the choice, tasks that need nearly every token, such as counting occurrences across a long document, defeat top-k selection.

blocks.md:
**When any top-k scheme struggles.** Selection works when a few keys carry the answer. Aggregation tasks spread it over the whole context: counting how often a word appears across a long document needs every occurrence, and dropping 80% of tokens drops most of them. MagicPIG's authors showed exactly this on RULER, a long-context benchmark: exact top-k attention on a dense model kept its accuracy on needle-in-a-haystack retrieval but degraded severely on common-word and frequent-word extraction. Their fix was to sample keys with LSH rather than keep only the top ones. Native training helps a model use its selector well, but it cannot make a 2048-token selection see 100,000 occurrences.

Rule of thumb: pretraining from scratch, consider NSA-style native training; adapting a dense checkpoint, add a cheap selector and keep training (DSA, MoBA, InfLLM-v2); with no training budget, use a training-free decode-time selector such as Quest; and test aggregation tasks, not only retrieval.

The NSA ideas that recur across these designs: choose by content, read memory in units the GPU handles well (blocks of tokens, or whole 576-number cached rows in DSA), let heads that share a KV cache agree on one selection (MoBA as described is the exception), and train with the sparsity. Window and initial-block safety nets appear in NSA and InfLLM-v2 but not in DSA. What varies most is how blocks or tokens are scored and whether new parameters are added.

blocks.question: A team adds MoBA-style block selection to a dense GQA model with 8 query heads per KV head, each head choosing its own top-4 blocks by mean-pooled keys. Decode latency barely improves. What should they change first?
options: Use a larger block size
Replace mean pooling with an MLP
Make the heads of each group share one selection, for example by summing or averaging their block scores as NSA and InfLLM-v2 do
Turn off the forced current block
blocks.explain: Decoding is memory bound, and heads in a group share one KV cache, so independent picks load the union of up to 32 blocks. Summing (NSA) or averaging (InfLLM-v2) scores over the group and taking one top-4 keeps loads at 4 blocks. Block size and scoring function do not fix the union problem.

blocks.question: Which task is most likely to defeat a sparse attention model that keeps 2048 of 100,000 context tokens per query?
options: Answering a question whose answer sits in one paragraph
Counting how many times a given word appears across the whole document
Continuing the last sentence
Copying a phone number mentioned once near the start
blocks.explain: Retrieval and local continuation need a few keys, which top-k finds. Counting needs every occurrence; if the word appears thousands of times, a 2048-token selection cannot hold them all. MagicPIG measured this kind of degradation for exact top-k attention on RULER's word-extraction tasks.

blocks.question: Reformer's LSH attention and the Routing Transformer's k-means attention both choose keys by content. Which problem from lesson 1 do they share that NSA avoids?
options: They cannot run on GPUs
Their bucket or cluster choice is discrete, so the loss does not train it directly, and the chosen keys are scattered in memory
They have quadratic cost
They only work for encoders
blocks.explain: Hash buckets and cluster assignments are discrete jumps with no gradient (Routing Transformer updates its centroids with k-means, not by the loss), and their members sit anywhere in the sequence. NSA scores contiguous blocks with a compression branch that the loss trains through its own output.
